title: Wounded drug-gang thug dies
article: An Asian-based gang member wounded by police during a shootout Wednesday has died.
Police say Long Duy Hoang, known on the street as "Crazy Jimmy," was a mid-level "enforcer" in one of Edmonton's notorious drug gangs. He died in hospital Friday.

Autopsy results released by police show he died of gunshot wounds. Edmonton Police Service spokesperson Sgt. Bryan Boulanger said Hoang had been "struck multiple times." Police say he was shot after he opened fire on several officers following a high-speed chase that ended in a crash.

Hoang is the first person to be shot and killed by an Edmonton police officer in the line of duty in 10 years. Police killed Erwin Harrison Adams, 27, in 1990 after he threatened family members and police with knives.

According to police sources, Hoang belonged to one of Edmonton's two rival Asian-based gangs. He was well-known to police as an enforcer who doled out discipline, but he was not a high-ranking player.
A few police officers said they fear retribution from Hoang's gang.

"Yeah, I definitely have some concerns with it," said one long\- time officer. "Maybe someone else would like to make a name for themselves. And we are easier to pick off than you think. It's something that's always in the back of your mind, and this kind of pushes it forward."

The officer said he has taken some long, hard looks from a few dial-a-dopers lately and it makes him nervous. Dial-a-doper is the slang term for cellular-phone-carrying drug runners who operate within a larger gang network.
"It just reminds you of reality and says, \`keep your head up, be more careful,' " he said.
Police were not surprised when the violence escalated, he added.
"I believe our department has been very lucky. This is something I half expected. There are more and more guns on the street."

The officer has spoken with tactical-squad members who were involved in Wednesday night's shooting and said some of them are still shaken up by it. "Policemen aren't killers," he said. "Even when it's the bad guy, taking a life affects them. It's very difficult."
Another constable said the potential for retribution has crossed his mind, too, but added that police officers are always prime targets for angry criminals and their cohorts.
"It's always a possibility. They may try to intimidate us, you know, \`you shoot one of ours, we'll shoot one of yours' kind of thing."

A provincial court judge will conduct a fatality inquiry into Hoang's death some time this year, spokesperson Boulanger said. A use-of-force review board, made up of two deputy chiefs and three senior officers, will examine in detail what led to the police officers discharging their weapons. The review should be completed within a few weeks.
A criminal investigation, which will take weeks or months to complete, is also under way to determine if the shooting death of Hoang by police was justifiable.
Police were acting on two separate anonymous tips Wednesday when they put a west-end home and a Honda Accord parked out front under surveillance. Two men got into the car around 8 p.m.
After a brief chase the Honda crashed into a parked Jeep. Passenger Hoa Tran, 26, surrendered on order from police. According to police reports, Hoang, the driver, started shooting.
Three officers returned fire and Hoang was hit several times.
